title: Ousted and reinstated in 11 days: board claims national-security risks eliminated, produces no evidence
dek: In ten days, Nvidia's board transformed ‘launch a national-security investigation into Jensen Huang’ into ‘no national-security risks exist’, the only confirmed variable between: Trump's direct involvement. No investigation report, no data, no public evidence.
why: One episode distills a rare corporate-governance fiasco: classified intelligence, an affair, four trillion dollars in market value vanishing and reappearing, and the White House stepping in to rescue a CEO.
who: Founders and investors tracking AI-industry governance structures, tech-stock valuation swings, and how political power enters corporate decisions.

points.h: Only an irreplaceable CEO could regain his throne
points.body: After being ousted for 11 days, Huang was reinstated. Reporter Robbie Whelan explains why this fiasco shook the world: Nvidia stock is about 6% of the S&P 500, and Huang himself is seen as an ‘imperial CEO’—his personal image is so bound to the company that Silicon Valley commonly believes ‘without him the company makes no sense.’ This personality-cult governance structure was what made the reversal possible.

points.h: A definitive 'no' becomes 'yes' in six days, with zero explanation
points.body: On the November 17 earnings call, the board stated clearly they had ‘no plan to reinstate Huang’—this came after Huang himself announced he was willing to return. But just six days later, the board suddenly announced unanimously that he was back. The reporter stresses the reversal happened extremely fast, and the company's only explanation was a press release saying it was satisfied with Huang's ‘candor and leadership.’

points.h: Trump's direct pressure, not evidence, reversed the board's decision
points.body: The reporter is direct: within hours of the announcement, one thing was certain—this was largely about Trump. Trump revealed on CNBC that he had discussed Huang's reinstatement with Nvidia's board and said he ‘strongly felt he should come back.’ According to a U.S. official, Trump also asked VP Vance to assist. Trump said Huang had been ‘exonerated.’

points.h: An alleged spy becomes an ambitious entrepreneur, no new evidence
points.body: One person Huang was involved with is Alice Wong, a Chinese national. Her data-center company Megaspeed is under multiple federal investigations, suspected of smuggling high-performance AI chips to China. The government had initially focused on whether she was a trained spy, but this week external descriptions of her softened to ‘possibly just an ambitious tech entrepreneur caught in a complex situation.’ But the reporter stresses: this shift wasn't based on new evidence—the narrative itself changed.

points.h: The internal affair was the true reason for removal, then forgotten
points.body: According to the reporter, when the board first pushed for removal, the relationship with the alleged spy was ‘tolerable’—provided Huang didn't know her identity. But his affair with a subordinate at the company was what truly crossed the line. After the reinstatement announcement, almost no one asked about it again, suggesting the internal investigation was quietly shelved.

points.h: Markets boom while Congress receives neither answer nor evidence
points.body: The afternoon the announcement broke, Nvidia stock rose over 30%, the company's biggest single-day gain in history, with market value returning to about four trillion dollars. Meanwhile, criticism from Washington's center-left intensified, with Senator Warren and Republican Senator Cornyn publicly questioning: on what basis does the board say national-security risks have been eliminated? Where is the evidence?

points.h: One person's decisions shape how the entire AI industry borrows money
points.body: The reporter points out the reinstatement won't change fundamental uncertainty in AI-industry demand, but it will immediately ease short-term lending and financing, because Huang's personal decisions and will shape how the entire industry borrows, raises capital, and invests. During his brief absence, market confidence in the future nearly collapsed; as soon as he returned, ‘the game restarted.’

points.h: AI-company governance is so weak that outside pressure can override boards
points.body: The reporter compares this to OpenAI's previous ouster and swift reinstatement of Sam Altman, arguing it shows that tech, especially AI, has extremely weak corporate governance: board decisions can be ‘steamrolled’ by external forces—if enough people unite against a removal, it can be overturned. He thinks Wall Street worries this governance model is becoming normal.

terms.def: A CEO whose personal identity is so bound to the company that stakeholders believe it cannot function without them.
